card.title: Chess Log Tournament
card.content: Intuitive terminal based UI to automate chess tournament management: Round-robin pairings, live standings and easy-to-access data.
card.imageAlt: Image of the chess log app

descriptionContent: <bold>I built a small tool to run chess tournaments without juggling paper or manually creating pairings.</bold>

You select a match, enter results, and the standings update instantly. Starting a new round triggers automatic pairings using <bold>the circle method</bold>, with a slight bias toward the most interesting matches.

All data is stored in plain <bold>JSON</bold> files, non-technical users can easily export or modify the data. The whole interface is built with <bold>curses</bold>, which kept it fast and pleasant to use for a terminal environment.
imageAlt: List view of the available tournaments, with a new tournament popup.
Animated gif of the application in use, show a tournament in progress.
List view of the registered players.
imageText: Example of the software during a tournament
detail.whatILearnedTitle: Things I had to figure out along the way
whatILearnedContent: <bold>MVC architecture.</bold> Separating business logic, persistence, views, and user input.
<bold>Pairing logic.</bold> Generating matches that avoid repeats while prioritizing strong pairings. Implemented using the circle method.
<bold>Terminal UI.</bold> Making a text-based interface feel structured and navigable with window layouts and keyboard controls.
<bold>Early-stage Python code.</bold> I wrote this in my first months learning Python. The code shows it, but the finished tool still represents an important learning milestone.

card.title: LITRevu Website
card.content: Request and publish book reviews with a personalized feed shaped by a follow/block system.

descriptionContent: <bold>A lightweight space to request reviews, write your own, and follow readers whose tastes echo yours.</bold>
Users can open review requests or respond to those posted by others. The feed adapts to each reader by using follow/block relationships to bring relevant content forward.
Built with <bold>Django</bold> on top of a <bold>SQLite</bold> database. Styling is written in <bold>SCSS</bold>, with small interactive features handled in <bold>JavaScript</bold>.
imageAlt: Gif of the website in action
whatILearnedContent: <bold>MVT architecture.</bold> Implemented views, routing, forms, authentication, and relational models behind user-driven features like follow/block.
<bold>Custom widgets.</bold> Created and customized Django form widgets by subclassing and overriding default behaviors.
<bold>Frontend foundations.</bold> First structured use of SCSS and small-scale JavaScript to support a more coherent user experience.
<bold>Class-based views.</bold> Explored Django’s CBVs for rapid development; their abstractions helped but required care to avoid hidden complexity.

card.title: SoftDesk API
card.content: REST API for managing projects, contributors, issues, and comments, with role-based permissions and filtered endpoints.

descriptionContent: <bold>An API designed to structure collaborative work: create projects, define contributors, track issues, and exchange feedback through comments.</bold>

Endpoints are protected with JWT authentication and fine-grained permissions. List routes support filtering to quickly retrieve the relevant entries. Only registered contributors can access a project's details and its nested resources.

Built with <bold>Django REST Framework</bold> on top of <bold>SQLite</bold>, using drf-nested-routers to expose clean nested endpoints (projects/1/issues/2/comments/3). A full Postman collection accompanies the project for testing and documentation.
imageAlt: A screenshot of the list view of Issues with the filter open.
Image of the body sent with a PUT request to modify an issue.
imageText: The filter in the web-based API
A body in the web browser
whatILearnedContent: <bold>DRF fundamentals.</bold> Worked with serializers, viewsets, relational models, and nested routing to structure complex resources.
<bold>Auth and permissions.</bold> Implemented JWT authentication and custom access rules so each project exposes only the data relevant to its contributors.
<bold>Documentation workflow.</bold> Produced a Postman collection describing each endpoint and typical interaction flows.

card.title: Epic Events CRM
card.content: CLI-based CRM built with hexagonal architecture, managing clients, contracts and events with strict permissions and transactional integrity.
card.imageAlt: Screenshot of the eecrm command line interface in action

descriptionContent: <bold>A terminal CRM designed to centralize clients, contracts, and event data in a cohesive, structured system.</bold>

The project applies <bold>DDD</bold> principles with clear separation between domain, services and infrastructure (database and interfaces). <bold>Repository</bold> and <bold>Unit of Work</bold> patterns operate data persistence and ensure transactional consistency without impacting the domain entities.

Uses <bold>SQLAlchemy (imperative)</bold> with <bold>PostgreSQL</bold> for persistence. Services operate on domain objects, committing changes through units of work. A custom decorator provides RBAC/ABAC-style fine-grained permissions, and logging is handled locally with forwarding to <bold>Sentry</bold> for unexpected errors.
whatILearnedContent: <bold>DDD-inspired design.</bold> Domain entities, application services, repositories and units of work structured around ideas from 'Architecture Patterns with Python' (Percival & Gregory).
<bold>Testing strategy.</bold> Extensive pytest suite with isolated fixtures, allowing service tests to run without a database and integration tests to verify transactional behavior.
<bold>Dependencies tools (uv).</bold> Packaging, dependency management and build workflows using uv and a clear pyproject.toml (entry points, test config, metadata).
<bold>Architectural discipline.</bold> This project clarified the advantages of decoupling; cleaner tests, predictable data flow and easier refactoring.

card.title: OC Lettings Pipeline
card.content: Automated CI/CD pipeline for a Django app: linting, tests, Docker image build, deployment to Render, and documentation rebuild.
card.imageAlt: Screenshot of a GitHub Actions workflow for the OC Lettings project

detail.descriptionTitle: From Git push to deployed app
descriptionContent: <bold>A CI/CD pipeline that takes an existing Django app from commit to production automatically.</bold>

On merges into the main branch, a <bold>GitHub Actions</bold> workflow runs linting and tests, builds two <bold>Docker</bold> images (clean and demo), pushes them to <bold>Docker Hub</bold>, and triggers a redeploy on <bold>Render</bold> via a deploy hook.
The pipeline also rebuilds the <bold>Sphinx</bold> documentation so that each release ships with up-to-date docs, keeping the application, container images, and documentation aligned.
imageAlt: Read the Docs documentation index page
detail.whatILearnedTitle: Automating delivery of a Django app
whatILearnedContent: <bold>GitHub Actions CI/CD.</bold> Designed a workflow with separate jobs for linting, tests, Docker builds, image pushes, and deployment via a web hook, using secrets and environment variables.
<bold>Containerization.</bold> Built small sized Docker images for different data states (clean and demo), pushed them to Docker Hub.
<bold>Deployment.</bold> Automated redeploys to wire an image with an embedded database to a Render service for demonstration purposes.
<bold>Documentation automation.</bold> Integrated Sphinx documentation so it is rebuilt and republished on each pipeline run, keeping technical docs synchronized with the deployed version.
<bold>Quality check.</bold> Used pytest and linters in the pipeline as mandatory checks for merging on the main branch so that only passing code reaches the deployment step.
